title: WHY DO CHRISTIAN COUPLES STOP DATING AFTER MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: WHY DO CHRISTIAN COUPLES STOP DATING AFTER MARRIAGE?

You prayed for each other. You pursued each other. You counted the hours until you could be together. Then somewhere between the wedding vows, bills, children, ministry, exhaustion, and ordinary life… the person you once pursued became the person you simply assumed would always be there.
There was probably a time when you couldn't wait to see them.
You remembered what made them laugh.
You stayed up too late talking because somehow sleep seemed less important than hearing one more story from the person you loved.
“Lord, if this is the person You have for me…”
And slowly, almost invisibly, something changed.
You still ask who is picking up the children.
You may still sit beside each other at church.
You might even hold hands during prayer.
But when was the last time you looked at your husband or wife and thought:
Not remind you what needs to be done.
Because one of the quiet dangers of marriage is believing that familiarity means there is nothing left to discover.
And perhaps that is why some Christian couples stop dating after marriage.
They misunderstand what the wedding accomplished.
Marriage is not the finish line of pursuit.
It is the covenant in which pursuit is supposed to deepen.
Scripture never commands married couples to maintain a modern cultural ritual called “date night.” We should be careful not to turn helpful relationship practices into commandments God never gave.
But Scripture says something far deeper.
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew word translated “cleave” is דָּבַק — dabaq.
It carries the sense of clinging, adhering, holding fast, staying joined.
Not merely existing under the same roof.
Not simply maintaining legal marital status.
There is movement in that word.
A refusal to casually release what covenant has joined.
And that matters because many marriages do not collapse in one spectacular moment.
One postponed conversation at a time.
One distracted dinner at a time.
One evening spent staring into separate screens at a time.
One unresolved wound at a time.
One “we’ll talk later” at a time.
Until two people can sleep inches apart while feeling miles away.
You can know your spouse’s coffee order and stop knowing their fears.
You can know their schedule and stop knowing their heart.
You can know the password to their phone and have no idea what they have been crying about when nobody is watching.
You can become incredibly efficient at running a household while becoming strangers inside it.
And because there may be no affair, no screaming, no divorce papers, no dramatic scandal, everybody assumes everything is fine.
But neglect does not always announce itself.
But knowing someone loves you and experiencing that love are not always the same thing.
This is where Christian marriage must become unmistakably Christ-centered.
The Greek command translated “love” comes from ἀγαπάω — agapaō.
This is not merely romantic chemistry.
It is active, intentional love expressed for the good of another.
And then Paul gives Christian husbands an astonishing standard:
How did Christ love His church?
That means biblical marital love cannot survive indefinitely on the question:
And sometimes something as ordinary as putting the phone away and saying:
Dating your spouse after marriage does not have to mean expensive restaurants, flowers every Friday, luxury hotels, elaborate vacations, or carefully staged photographs.
Some couples genuinely cannot afford those things.
Some are caring for elderly parents.
Some are walking through sickness, unemployment, grief, disability, financial hardship, or seasons where simply making it through the week feels exhausting.
You can sit on the porch together.
Share coffee after the children fall asleep.
Ask questions you have not asked in years.
You can look across the kitchen table at the person you married and say:
“What has been heavy on your heart lately?”
Maybe romance sometimes looks less like candlelight and more like undivided attention.
Because attention has become expensive in a distracted world.
And your spouse notices where yours goes.
There is another uncomfortable reason married couples sometimes stop pursuing one another.
Before marriage, flaws can seem small because affection is enormous.
After years together, the flaws can appear enormous because familiarity has made affection lazy.
The little habit that once seemed cute becomes irritating.
The personality difference that once fascinated you becomes exhausting.
You remember the argument from three years ago.
You remember the apology you believe was never sincere enough.
And suddenly you are not dating your spouse anymore.
Yet Christian marriage places two sinners inside one covenant.
That means marriage will eventually require something romance alone cannot provide.
“Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.”
Because before I obsess over everything my spouse needs to repent of, the Gospel reminds me that I am someone who desperately needed mercy too.
Marriage is not the union of two flawless people.
It is the covenant of two people who need Jesus.
Two people capable of saying cruel things.
Two people who sometimes misunderstand each other.
Two people who can be astonishingly immature five minutes after reading the Bible.
And two people whom Christ can continually transform.

This does not mean tolerating abuse, coercion, violence, manipulation, or dangerous behavior. Biblical forgiveness should never be twisted into a command to remain silently exposed to harm. Serious situations may require safety, pastoral wisdom, professional counseling, medical help, or appropriate civil authorities.
Grace is not pretending evil is good.
Forgiveness is not calling destruction love.
But in ordinary marital conflict, there is something profoundly Christian about two imperfect people repeatedly returning to humility.
Those words can save years of distance.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to say them tonight.
Because pride has already stolen enough evenings.
The Song of Songs also destroys the strange idea that marital affection becomes somehow less spiritual after the wedding.
Scripture portrays covenant love with delight, longing, admiration, exclusivity, tenderness, and desire.
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.”
The Hebrew word often translated “beloved” is דּוֹדִי — dodi.
Somewhere beneath the schedules, responsibilities, disagreements, diapers, dishes, deadlines, mortgages, ministry meetings, and accumulated disappointments…
But perhaps tonight God is not asking you to manufacture some artificial version of your honeymoon.
Maybe He is simply exposing the distance you stopped noticing.
Because there is a terrifying moment in some marriages when loneliness becomes normal.
You stop asking why you do not talk anymore.
You stop reaching because rejection hurts.
You stop apologizing because every argument feels repetitive.
You stop planning time together because something always interrupts it.
Routine may be part of marriage.
But emotional neglect should not be romanticized as maturity.
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
Marriage was never designed merely to produce two exhausted roommates who share expenses and occasionally attend church together.
Your spouse is a human soul.
Still carrying memories you do not completely understand.
You have not finished knowing them.
And they have not finished knowing you.
That is why continuing to “date” your spouse can be much more than preserving romance.
It can be an act of curiosity.
“I refuse to assume I already know everything about you.”
Ask your wife what she dreams about now.
Not what she dreamed about when you were twenty-three.
Ask your husband what has been frightening him lately.
Ask what has made your spouse feel unseen.
Ask when they feel closest to you.
Ask what they miss about the beginning of your relationship.
Ask where you have wounded them.
Then be brave enough not to defend yourself immediately.
There may be things you did not want to hear.
But sometimes healing begins when somebody finally feels safe enough to tell the truth.
And perhaps this article is landing painfully because you know exactly when the distance began.
After one of you became consumed with work.
After ministry became more important than the marriage.
After the words were spoken that neither of you could take back.
And now “go on a date” sounds painfully simplistic.
Some wounds cannot be repaired over dinner.
Some marriages need much more than romance.
And sometimes a long rebuilding of trust.
But even there, the Gospel speaks.
Because Christianity is built around a truth scandalous enough to offend human pride:
Broken things are not beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
The cross itself looked like the end.
A stone rolled across the entrance.
Except Jesus specializes in stories everybody else thinks are finished.
And while marriage is not the Gospel and no earthly marriage is promised a painless outcome, Christian hope means brokenness does not have to have the final word.
Maybe your marriage has a chapter you wish nobody knew.
Maybe you have been pretending at church.
Maybe everyone sees the smiling Facebook photographs while you know what the house feels like after the camera is gone.
And Christ does not call sinners into hiding.
He calls us into the light.
The answer is not pretending your marriage is perfect.
The answer is bringing the truth before Jesus.
Maybe your next date should begin before you ever leave the house.
“I think I have taken you for granted.”
“I've been physically present but emotionally absent.”
“I want Christ to become the center of our marriage again.”
And perhaps the most beautiful answer will not be dramatic.
Maybe your spouse simply reaches across the table.
Maybe rebuilding feels slower than you hoped.
But small acts of faithfulness matter.
You do not rebuild ten years of distance in ten minutes.
You begin with the next faithful step.
Seek help when you need it.
Remember the person behind the responsibilities.
Jesus is not merely interested in making your marriage more romantic.
He wants to make you more like Him.
Marriage can expose selfishness with ruthless precision.
Our hunger to be served instead of serving.
And those revelations can feel scandalous.
But exposure in the hands of Christ can become an invitation to grace.
Because Jesus did not go to the cross for the polished version of you.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we learned how to be perfect husbands and wives.
That is the foundation beneath every Christian marriage.
So if this article exposed something uncomfortable, do not waste that conviction.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to know that another chapter can still be written.
Not because sharing a post somehow earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because you need another post buried in a folder.
There may come a night when you are angry.
A night when you feel invisible.
A night when both of you are exhausted and you begin wondering where the people in those wedding photographs went.
Your spouse is not merely the person helping you survive adulthood.
A soul entrusted to your covenant love.
And perhaps tonight you do not need an expensive reservation.
Maybe you just need two chairs.
“I don't want us to become strangers.”
Because maybe the marriage you thought was simply growing old has actually been waiting for someone to start pursuing again.

And maybe years from now, when somebody asks when everything began changing, you will remember an ordinary night when pride finally surrendered, two hearts became honest, and Jesus was invited into the rooms you had kept locked.

Sometimes the most romantic thing you can do is look again at the person you promised never to stop choosing—and choose them again under the grace of the Christ who first chose to love sinners like you.
